name: Coahuitlán Totonac

catalog_quote: Stress is predictable in most monomorphemic roots based on the weight of the final syllable. When the final syllable of a word is heavy, this syllable takes stress, when the final syllable is light, the word takes penultimate stress. In Coahuitlán Totonac, a heavy syllable is one that contains a long vowel (54), or is closed by a sonorant consonant (55). ... In these examples, the final syllable is heavy which results in word-final stress. A light syllable contains a short vowel (56), or is closed by an obstruent consonant (57). ... Ending in light syllables, these words receive penultimate stress. One exception to this rule of syllable weight concerns glottal stops: although they are not sonorants, syllables ending in glottal stops are also considered heavy and take final stress, (58). ... audit.reasoning: The record rests on the only modern description of Coahuitlán Totonac, a 2024 fieldwork dissertation with a dedicated stress section, held in full and quoted verbatim at the stated pages (pp.70-72). The classification (weight-sensitive final/penult window; heavy = Vː(C)#, VC[+son]#, Vʔ#; light = V#, VC[-son]#; morphological overrides liː- and compounds) matches the source exactly, including footnote 18's sonorant inventory. Glottolog lists no descriptive references for this languoid, and a web search of the UAlberta Totonac project, CJL and OWPIL turned up only Moore's syntax and subgrouping papers, which are silent on stress (Moore 2017 downloaded and checked). No better or competing source exists, so no works still to obtain and no action.
